blocks.en: 1. The Choir That Was Late
blocks.es_reference: 1. El coro que llegó tarde

blocks.en: On Wednesday, March 1, 1950, the choir of West Side Baptist Church in Beatrice, Nebraska, was supposed to start rehearsal at 7:20 in the evening. The choir always came early. They never missed. But that night, fifteen singers had fifteen separate reasons to be late. The pianist’s nap ran long. A high-school sophomore was stuck on her homework. One couple’s car would not start. The pastor and his wife were delayed. At about 7:20, the choir loft was empty for the first time in anyone’s memory.
blocks.es_reference: El miércoles 1 de marzo de 1950, el coro de la Iglesia Bautista del Lado Oeste en Beatrice, Nebraska, debía comenzar su ensayo a las 7:20 de la noche. El coro siempre llegaba temprano. Nunca faltaban. Pero esa noche, quince cantantes tuvieron quince razones distintas para llegar tarde. La siesta de la pianista se prolongó. Una estudiante de secundaria estaba atorada con su tarea. El auto de una pareja no encendía. El pastor y su esposa se retrasaron. Hacia las 7:20, el coro estaba vacío por primera vez en la memoria de cualquiera.

blocks.en: Minutes later, a gas leak in the basement of West Side Baptist found the church furnace, and the whole building blew up. The furnace room sat directly beneath the choir loft. Nobody died. Fifteen unrelated small inconveniences had pulled fifteen people out of a death zone on the one night it mattered.
blocks.es_reference: Minutos después, una fuga de gas en el sótano de la Bautista del Lado Oeste encontró la caldera de la iglesia, y todo el edificio explotó. La sala de la caldera estaba directamente debajo del coro. Nadie murió. Quince inconvenientes pequeños sin relación entre sí habían sacado a quince personas de una zona de muerte la única noche en que importaba.

blocks.en: Take any one of those fifteen events alone — a homework problem, a balky car, a long nap — and it means nothing. Read them all together, and you see God’s providence at work. Context changes the meaning. The same is true of every verse of the Bible. Pulled out of its setting, it can be made to say almost anything. Read within the paragraph, the chapter, the book, and the canon, it says what its Author intended. That is the discipline of this unit.
blocks.es_reference: Tome cualquiera de aquellos quince eventos por sí solo — un problema de tarea, un auto que no arranca, una siesta larga — y no significa nada. Léalos todos juntos, y verá la providencia de Dios obrando. El contexto cambia el significado. Lo mismo sucede con cada versículo de la Biblia. Sacado de su entorno, puede hacerse decir casi cualquier cosa. Leído dentro del párrafo, del capítulo, del libro, y del canon, dice lo que su Autor quiso decir. Ésa es la disciplina de esta unidad.

blocks.en: 2. The Pastor’s Hardest Word
blocks.es_reference: 2. La palabra más dura del pastor

blocks.en: The hardest word a pastor must say to himself before Sunday is one syllable long: wait. Wait before applying. Wait before quoting. Wait before turning the page. The verse you are about to preach was given inside a paragraph, that was given inside a chapter, that was given inside a book, that was given to a particular people at a particular time. Each frame carries weight. Skip any one of them and you risk preaching a sentence the Author never said.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra más dura que un pastor debe decirse a sí mismo antes del domingo es muy corta: espera. Espera antes de aplicar. Espera antes de citar. Espera antes de pasar la página. El versículo que está a punto de predicar fue dado dentro de un párrafo, que fue dado dentro de un capítulo, que fue dado dentro de un libro, que fue dado a un pueblo particular en un tiempo particular. Cada marco lleva peso. Sáltese cualquiera y se arriesga a predicar una frase que el Autor nunca dijo.

blocks.en: In this unit we will learn five layers of context: immediate, book, historical, cultural, and canonical. Each is a frame around the verse. The pastor’s job is to make sure all five frames hang square before he hammers a nail into the wall of his sermon. We will use one book — Esther — to see all five at work.
blocks.es_reference: En esta unidad aprenderemos cinco capas de contexto: el inmediato, el del libro, el histórico, el cultural, y el canónico. Cada uno es un marco alrededor del versículo. El trabajo del pastor es asegurarse de que los cinco marcos cuelguen rectos antes de clavar un solo clavo en la pared de su sermón. Usaremos un libro — Ester — para ver los cinco en acción.

blocks.en: 3. Immediate Context — The Verses Right Next Door
blocks.es_reference: 3. El contexto inmediato: los versículos vecinos

blocks.en: The first frame is the verses on either side. Cover the verse you are studying with your hand. Read what comes before. Read what comes after. The paragraph almost always tells you what the verse means, because the writer put the verse there for a reason.
blocks.es_reference: El primer marco son los versículos a uno y otro lado. Cubra con la mano el versículo que está estudiando. Lea lo que viene antes. Lea lo que viene después. El párrafo casi siempre le dice lo que significa el versículo, porque el escritor lo puso allí por una razón.

blocks.en: Consider Jeremiah 29:11. The verse itself reads beautifully:
blocks.es_reference: Considere Jeremías 29:11. El versículo en sí mismo se lee con belleza:

blocks.en: “For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, says the LORD, thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope.” (Jeremiah 29:11, NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: «Porque yo sé los pensamientos que tengo acerca de vosotros, dice Jehová, pensamientos de paz, y no de mal, para daros el fin que esperáis.» (Jeremías 29:11, RVG)

blocks.en: Lift that verse out of its paragraph and it becomes a refrigerator magnet. It promises prosperity to anyone who claims it. But back up two verses. Jeremiah is writing to Jewish exiles in Babylon. God has just told them through Jeremiah that they will be in captivity for seventy years. Most of them will die in a foreign land. The promise of peace and a future is given to a generation that will not live to enjoy it — it is a promise to their grandchildren.
blocks.es_reference: Saque ese versículo de su párrafo y se vuelve un imán de refrigerador. Promete prosperidad a cualquiera que lo reclame. Pero retroceda dos versículos. Jeremías está escribiendo a exiliados judíos en Babilonia. Dios acaba de decirles por medio de Jeremías que estarán en cautiverio durante setenta años. La mayoría morirá en tierra extraña. La promesa de paz y un futuro es dada a una generación que no vivirá para disfrutarla — es una promesa para sus nietos.

blocks.en: The verse is glorious, but it is not what the prosperity teacher claims. Honored in context, it teaches a long-suffering church to trust God across generations. Pulled out of context, it becomes a vending-machine ticket. Same words. Two different verses. Only one is what God said.
blocks.es_reference: El versículo es glorioso, pero no es lo que reclama el predicador de la prosperidad. Honrado en su contexto, enseña a una iglesia que sufre con paciencia a confiar en Dios a través de las generaciones. Sacado de contexto, se vuelve un boleto de máquina expendedora. Las mismas palabras. Dos versículos distintos. Solo uno es lo que dijo Dios.

blocks.en: 4. Book Context — What Is the Whole Book About?
blocks.es_reference: 4. El contexto del libro: ¿de qué trata todo el libro?

blocks.en: The second frame is the entire book in which the verse lives. Every book of the Bible has a main theme, a controlling argument, a purpose. Romans is not Psalms. Proverbs is not Revelation. Hebrews is not Job. Before you preach any verse, ask: What is the writer doing in this book? What problem is he trying to solve? What truth is he driving home?
blocks.es_reference: El segundo marco es el libro entero en el cual vive el versículo. Cada libro de la Biblia tiene un tema principal, un argumento gobernante, un propósito. Romanos no es Salmos. Proverbios no es Apocalipsis. Hebreos no es Job. Antes de predicar cualquier versículo, pregunte: ¿qué está haciendo el escritor en este libro? ¿Qué problema está tratando de resolver? ¿Qué verdad está martillando?

blocks.en: Consider the book of Esther. The name of God is never mentioned. Not once. There is no prayer recorded, no temple, no priest, no sacrifice. Read in isolation, it looks like a court-intrigue novel. Read as a whole book, you see what Esther is doing — teaching God’s scattered people that their silent God is still their providential God. The whole point of the book is what God does when He says nothing. Miss that, and every chapter becomes a moral fable. Catch it, and the book preaches itself.
blocks.es_reference: Considere el libro de Ester. El nombre de Dios nunca se menciona. Ni una vez. No hay oración registrada, no hay templo, no hay sacerdote, no hay sacrificio. Leído aislado, parece una novela de intriga palaciega. Leído como libro entero, usted ve lo que Ester está haciendo — enseñar al pueblo disperso de Dios que su Dios silencioso sigue siendo su Dios providente. El punto entero del libro es lo que Dios hace cuando no dice nada. Pierda eso, y cada capítulo se vuelve una fábula moral. Capte eso, y el libro se predica solo.

blocks.en: 5. Historical Context — Who Was There, and When?
blocks.es_reference: 5. El contexto histórico: ¿quién estaba allí, y cuándo?

blocks.en: The third frame is history. Each book of the Bible was written into a real moment, with real kings, real wars, real exiles, real famines. The pastor who skips the history reads the words but misses the weight.
blocks.es_reference: El tercer marco es la historia. Cada libro de la Biblia fue escrito dentro de un momento real, con reyes reales, guerras reales, exilios reales, hambrunas reales. El pastor que se salta la historia lee las palabras pero pierde el peso.

blocks.en: Esther takes place around 480 B.C. in the Persian Empire. The Jews are in exile. Some have returned to rebuild Jerusalem, but most are still scattered across 127 provinces under the Persian king Xerxes — from the borders of Egypt to the borders of India. Haman is a descendant of the Amalekites, the very tribe that opposed Israel when they first approached the Promised Land a thousand years earlier. The hatred has a history. When you know the history, Haman’s plot to exterminate the Jews is not random villainy. It is one more chapter in a war that began near Sinai. The history makes the danger feel real.
blocks.es_reference: Ester ocurre alrededor del año 480 a.C. en el Imperio Persa. Los judíos están en el exilio. Algunos han regresado a reconstruir Jerusalén, pero la mayoría sigue dispersa por 127 provincias bajo el rey persa Asuero — desde las fronteras de Egipto hasta las fronteras de la India. Amán es descendiente de los amalecitas, la misma tribu que se opuso a Israel cuando se acercaban por primera vez a la Tierra Prometida mil años antes. El odio tiene una historia. Cuando usted conoce la historia, el complot de Amán para exterminar a los judíos no es maldad al azar. Es un capítulo más en una guerra que comenzó cerca de Sinaí. La historia hace que el peligro se sienta real.

blocks.en: A theologian was once asked, “Can you prove the existence of God?” He answered in two words: the Jew. The Egyptians, the Philistines, the Babylonians, the Persians, the Greeks, the Romans, the Crusaders, the Spanish, the Nazis — every great empire has tried to wipe out God’s people, and not one has succeeded. The same Hand that thwarted Haman has thwarted every successor. The pastor who has read his history preaches Esther differently.
blocks.es_reference: A un teólogo le preguntaron una vez: «¿Puede usted probar la existencia de Dios?» Respondió en dos palabras: los judíos. Los egipcios, los filisteos, los babilonios, los persas, los griegos, los romanos, los cruzados, los españoles, los nazis — cada gran imperio ha tratado de exterminar al pueblo de Dios, y ninguno lo ha logrado. La misma Mano que frustró a Amán ha frustrado a cada sucesor. El pastor que ha leído su historia predica Ester de otra manera.

blocks.en: 6. Cultural Context — How Did They Live?
blocks.es_reference: 6. El contexto cultural: ¿cómo vivían?

blocks.en: The fourth frame is culture. What did the original readers wear, eat, fear, and assume? What customs shaped their world?
blocks.es_reference: El cuarto marco es la cultura. ¿Qué llevaban puesto, qué comían, qué temían, y qué daban por sentado los lectores originales? ¿Qué costumbres moldeaban su mundo?

blocks.en: In Esther 4 the queen tells Mordecai she cannot simply walk in and speak to her husband. In the Persian court, no person — not even the queen — could enter the king’s presence uninvited. If the king did not extend his golden scepter, the visitor was put to death. The modern reader hears Esther say, “If I perish, I perish,” and may think she is being dramatic. The original reader knew she meant it literally. Cultural context restores the weight of the word.
blocks.es_reference: En Ester 4 la reina le dice a Mardoqueo que no puede simplemente entrar y hablar con su marido. En la corte persa, ninguna persona — ni siquiera la reina — podía entrar a la presencia del rey sin ser invitada. Si el rey no extendía su cetro de oro, el visitante era condenado a muerte. El lector moderno oye a Ester decir, «si perezco, que perezca», y puede pensar que está siendo dramática. El lector original sabía que lo decía literalmente. El contexto cultural restaura el peso de la palabra.

blocks.en: The same is true when the king cannot sleep one night and asks for the royal chronicles to be read aloud. To us this is curious; to a Persian, this was normal — kings often had clerks read official records aloud as a sleep aid. What looks like a quirk of insomnia was a routine palace habit. And on that one particular night, the clerk happened to read about a Jewish guard named Mordecai who had saved the king’s life years before and never been thanked. Once you know the culture, that scene shifts from accident to providence.
blocks.es_reference: Lo mismo sucede cuando el rey no puede dormir una noche y pide que le lean las crónicas reales en voz alta. Para nosotros eso es curioso; para un persa, era normal — los reyes muchas veces hacían que los escribas leyeran los registros oficiales en voz alta como remedio para dormir. Lo que parece una rareza del insomnio era una costumbre rutinaria del palacio. Y en aquella noche particular, sucedió que el escriba leyó acerca de un guardia judío llamado Mardoqueo que había salvado la vida del rey años antes y a quien nunca habían dado las gracias. Una vez que usted conoce la cultura, esa escena pasa de accidente a providencia.

blocks.en: 7. Canonical Context — The Whole Bible Around the Verse
blocks.es_reference: 7. El contexto canónico: la Biblia entera alrededor del versículo

blocks.en: The fifth and largest frame is the canonical one. Every verse of the Bible lives inside the Bible. No verse is an island. Sometimes the meaning of a passage cannot be settled by its own paragraph alone — it needs the rest of Scripture to hold it in place. We saw this in our last unit, when Satan misused Psalm 91 and Jesus answered with Deuteronomy 6. That is canonical context at work.
blocks.es_reference: El quinto y mayor marco es el canónico. Cada versículo de la Biblia vive dentro de la Biblia. Ningún versículo es una isla. A veces el significado de un pasaje no puede resolverse por su propio párrafo solamente — necesita el resto de la Escritura para sostenerlo en su lugar. Vimos esto en nuestra última unidad, cuando Satanás malusó el Salmo 91 y Jesús respondió con Deuteronomio 6. Ese es el contexto canónico en acción.

blocks.en: Esther itself only becomes fully clear when read against the rest of the canon. The promise that runs underneath Esther is the covenant promise to Abraham in Genesis 12: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. Haman curses Abraham’s people; Haman swings from his own gallows. The covenant operates silently through the whole story. A pastor who has only Esther in front of him sees a clever reversal. A pastor who has all sixty-six books in front of him sees Genesis 12 keeping its word two thousand years later.
blocks.es_reference: Ester mismo solo se vuelve plenamente claro cuando se lee contra el resto del canon. La promesa que corre por debajo de Ester es la promesa del pacto a Abraham en Génesis 12: Bendeciré a los que te bendijeren, y a los que te maldijeren maldeciré. Amán maldice al pueblo de Abraham; Amán se balancea en su propia horca. El pacto opera silenciosamente a lo largo de toda la historia. Un pastor que solo tiene a Ester delante ve una astuta inversión. Un pastor que tiene los sesenta y seis libros delante ve a Génesis 12 cumpliendo su palabra dos mil años después.

blocks.en: This is what we mean by “Scripture interprets Scripture.” The Bible is one book. Its parts speak to each other. The pastor who has read all of it preaches any of it more faithfully.
blocks.es_reference: Esto es lo que queremos decir con «la Escritura interpreta a la Escritura». La Biblia es un solo libro. Sus partes se hablan entre sí. El pastor que ha leído toda la Biblia predica cualquier parte de ella con mayor fidelidad.

blocks.en: 8. The Lower Story and the Upper Story
blocks.es_reference: 8. La historia de abajo y la historia de arriba

blocks.en: Run those five frames together and you get a picture I have come to call the lower story and the upper story. In Esther, the lower story is what everyone in the palace can see — a king with insomnia, a queen with courage, a courtier with ambition, a guard who once happened to overhear an assassination plot. The upper story is what only God sees from above — a covenant keeping itself, a people preserved, a Messiah’s genealogy protected so that a Savior could be born to Abraham’s line many centuries later.
blocks.es_reference: Corra esos cinco marcos juntos y obtendrá un cuadro que he llegado a llamar la historia de abajo y la historia de arriba. En Ester, la historia de abajo es lo que todos en el palacio pueden ver — un rey con insomnio, una reina con valor, un cortesano con ambición, un guardia que en cierta ocasión oyó por casualidad un complot de asesinato. La historia de arriba es lo que solo Dios ve desde lo alto — un pacto guardándose a sí mismo, un pueblo preservado, una genealogía mesiánica protegida para que un Salvador pudiera nacer del linaje de Abraham muchos siglos después.

blocks.en: Every verse in the Bible has both stories. The exegete’s job is to see both. The pastor who preaches only the lower story produces moralism — be brave like Esther. The pastor who preaches only the upper story produces abstraction — God’s sovereignty as a doctrine without a face. The pastor who preaches both gives his people history with heaven inside it.
blocks.es_reference: Cada versículo de la Biblia tiene ambas historias. El trabajo del exégeta es ver las dos. El pastor que predica solo la historia de abajo produce moralismo — sea valiente como Ester. El pastor que predica solo la historia de arriba produce abstracción — la soberanía de Dios como una doctrina sin rostro. El pastor que predica ambas le da a su pueblo historia con cielo adentro.

blocks.en: When Mordecai said to Esther, Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this? he was preaching the upper story into the lower. He could not have proved God was present — the book never lets us see God’s face. But he knew. Esther knew. And every reader of Esther, by the end of the book, knows.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Mardoqueo le dijo a Ester: ¿y quién sabe si para esta hora has llegado al reino?, estaba predicando la historia de arriba dentro de la de abajo. No podía probar que Dios estaba presente — el libro nunca nos deja ver el rostro de Dios. Pero él sabía. Ester sabía. Y cada lector de Ester, al terminar el libro, lo sabe.

blocks.en: 9. What Context Saves Us From
blocks.es_reference: 9. De qué nos salva el contexto

blocks.en: The discipline of context saves the pastor from four serious errors. From proof-texting — lifting verses out to support ideas they were never meant to support. From moralizing — turning every Bible story into a list of life lessons stripped of its place in God’s plan. From chronological flattening — treating commands given to Israel in the wilderness as if they were given to a small church in Mexico in our own day. And from cultural projection — reading our customs and values back into the lives of people who did not share them.
blocks.es_reference: La disciplina del contexto salva al pastor de cuatro errores serios. Del uso de versículos sueltos como prueba — levantar versículos para apoyar ideas que nunca debieron apoyar. Del moralismo — convertir cada historia bíblica en una lista de lecciones de vida despojadas de su lugar en el plan de Dios. Del aplanamiento cronológico — tratar mandamientos dados a Israel en el desierto como si fueran dados a una iglesia pequeña de México en nuestros propios días. Y de la proyección cultural — leer nuestras costumbres y valores en las vidas de personas que no las compartían.

blocks.en: Each error is a way of skipping context. Each error puts the pastor where Satan stood at the temple in Matthew 4, quoting a verse that says what the speaker wants it to say. The cure is always the same: back up. Read more. Look around. Honor the frames the Author placed around His words.
blocks.es_reference: Cada error es una manera de saltarse el contexto. Cada error pone al pastor donde estaba Satanás en el templo en Mateo 4, citando un versículo que dice lo que el hablante quiere que diga. La cura siempre es la misma: retroceda. Lea más. Mire alrededor. Honre los marcos que el Autor colocó alrededor de Sus palabras.

blocks.en: 10. Five Frames, One Week
blocks.es_reference: 10. Cinco marcos, una semana

blocks.en: Here is a practical schedule. Monday: read the immediate context — the chapter your text is in — out loud, twice, slowly. Tuesday: read the whole book, in one sitting if possible, asking what it is about. Wednesday: look up the historical setting in one good Bible handbook. Thursday: note any cultural detail the modern reader will miss — a custom, a coin, a court protocol, a season. Friday: trace the canonical thread — what earlier Scripture stands behind this text, and what later Scripture refers back to it.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí tiene un horario práctico. Lunes: lea el contexto inmediato — el capítulo donde está su texto — en voz alta, dos veces, despacio. Martes: lea el libro entero, en una sentada si es posible, preguntando de qué trata. Miércoles: busque el contexto histórico en un buen manual bíblico. Jueves: anote cualquier detalle cultural que el lector moderno pasará por alto — una costumbre, una moneda, un protocolo de la corte, una estación del año. Viernes: trace el hilo canónico — qué Escritura anterior está detrás de este texto, y qué Escritura posterior se refiere a él.

blocks.en: Saturday is for the sermon. By then, the five frames are hung. You can preach a single verse and know that the verse is saying what its Author intended — not because you are brilliant, but because you took the time to listen. The choir of West Side Baptist Church was saved by fifteen small interruptions on a single night. Your congregation will be saved by five small disciplines across one Bible week. The same Hand is at work.
blocks.es_reference: El sábado es para el sermón. Para entonces, los cinco marcos están colgados. Usted puede predicar un solo versículo y saber que el versículo está diciendo lo que su Autor quiso decir — no porque usted sea brillante, sino porque se tomó el tiempo para escuchar. El coro de la Bautista del Lado Oeste fue salvado por quince pequeñas interrupciones en una sola noche. Su congregación será salvada por cinco pequeñas disciplinas a lo largo de una semana bíblica. La misma Mano está obrando.

mc.why: Correct. Take any one of the 18 delays alone and it means nothing. Read them together and you see God's providence. Same with Bible verses: pulled out of context they can mean almost anything; read in context they say what the Author intended.

mc.stem: The lesson names five layers of context the pastor must honor. They are:
mc.why: Correct. Each frame surrounds the verse: the paragraph (immediate), the whole book, the historical moment, the cultural world, and the rest of Scripture (canonical). All five must hang square before the sermon is nailed up.

mc.stem: The hardest word a pastor must say to himself before Sunday, according to this lesson, is:
mc.why: Correct. Wait before applying. Wait before quoting. Wait before turning the page. Context demands patience. Skip any frame and you risk preaching a sentence the Author never said.

A passage that has no historical setting
A verse that means the same thing in any context
A verse that should never be quoted
mc.why: Correct. In context, Jeremiah 29:11 is given to exiles facing 70 more years of captivity — a promise to their grandchildren. Out of context, it becomes a prosperity-gospel slogan. Same words; two different verses; only one is what God said.

mc.stem: In its immediate context, Jeremiah 29:11 was originally addressed to:
options: New Testament believers in Asia Minor
Jewish exiles in Babylon facing seventy more years of captivity
mc.why: Correct. Two verses earlier, God tells the exiles through Jeremiah that they will be in captivity for seventy years. Most will die in a foreign land. The promise of peace is for the long haul — and largely for their grandchildren.

mc.stem: The lesson says the book of Esther is unusual because:
options: It is the only book written in Persian
It is the only book with two endings
The name of God is never mentioned in it
It is the shortest book of the Old Testament
mc.why: Correct. The name of God appears nowhere in Esther. No prayer, no temple, no priest, no sacrifice. The whole book teaches what God does when He says nothing — His silent providence behind the scenes. This is its book-context message.

mc.stem: Reading Esther at the level of book context reveals its main theme to be:
options: The silent God is still the providential God
The proper protocols for courtroom drama
mc.why: Correct. Read in isolation, Esther looks like court intrigue. Read as a whole book, it teaches God's scattered people that their silent God is still their providential God. That is the book context.

mc.stem: In the historical context of Esther, who was Haman?
options: A descendant of the Amalekites — Israel's ancient enemy
A converted Jew who had turned against his people
mc.why: Correct. Haman descended from the Amalekites — the tribe that opposed Israel a thousand years earlier near Sinai. Once you know the history, his plot is not random villainy; it is one more chapter in an ancient war.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, Esther's cultural context (Persian court protocol) gives weight to which famous line in her story?
options: "I will go in to the king, and if I perish, I perish"
"Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world"
"The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom"
mc.why: Correct. In Persian court protocol, even the queen risked death entering uninvited. The modern reader hears "if I perish, I perish" as dramatic. The original reader knew Esther meant it literally. Cultural context restores the weight.

mc.stem: The lesson explains the king's sleepless night and the reading of the royal chronicles (Esther 6) by appealing to:
options: A late addition to the book by Persian editors
Persian cultural custom — kings often had clerks read records aloud as a sleep aid
mc.why: Correct. To us a sleepless king reading chronicles seems quirky. To a Persian, it was routine — kings often had records read aloud to help them sleep. Cultural context turns what looks like coincidence into routine palace habit — and God's providence within it.

mc.stem: The canonical-context promise that runs underneath the whole book of Esther is:
options: The Abrahamic covenant in Genesis 12 — "I will curse him who curses you"
mc.why: Correct. Genesis 12:3 — "I will curse him who curses you." Haman curses Abraham's people; Haman swings from his own gallows. The covenant operates silently through the entire book. Canonical context reveals it.

mc.stem: The lesson calls the distinction between what people can see and what only God sees:
mc.why: Correct. The lower story is what the palace can see (insomnia, courage, ambition); the upper story is what God sees from above (a covenant keeping itself). Both are real. The pastor preaches both — neither moralism alone nor abstraction alone.

mc.stem: According to this lesson, a pastor who preaches only the lower story produces:
options: Mysticism — God removed from real events
mc.why: Correct. Lower-story-only preaching turns every Bible story into a life lesson stripped of God's plan. Be brave like Esther. Be wise like Solomon. Be patient like Job. Helpful, but flat — God Himself drops out of the picture.

mc.stem: According to this lesson, a pastor who preaches only the upper story produces:
options: Abstraction — God's sovereignty as a doctrine without a face
mc.why: Correct. Upper-story-only preaching reduces God's action to doctrine without flesh-and-blood human characters. The pastor must preach both stories: the lower so the people can recognize their own lives, the upper so they can recognize God's hand.

mc.stem: Mordecai's famous line to Esther — "Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" — illustrates:
options: Preaching the upper story into the lower
mc.why: Correct. Mordecai cannot prove God is acting — the book never lets us see God's face. But he names the upper story inside the lower-story situation. He preaches it into the moment, and Esther rises to it. So must we.

mc.stem: The lesson names four serious errors that the discipline of context saves the pastor from. They are:
options: Proof-texting, moralizing, chronological flattening, cultural projection
mc.why: Correct. Proof-texting (lifting verses out of their argument). Moralizing (stripping a story of God's plan). Chronological flattening (treating Sinai commands as if they were given to your church today). Cultural projection (reading our customs back into theirs).

mc.stem: The error of "chronological flattening" refers to:
options: Ignoring the order of New Testament books
Treating commands given to Israel in the wilderness as if given directly to a modern congregation
mc.why: Correct. Some commands were given to Israel under the law of Moses, others to the church under the new covenant. Treating them as flat — every command equally direct to every audience — collapses redemptive history and produces confusion.

mc.stem: The cure for the cult-twist of Bible verses (Mormons, JWs, prosperity teachers all using the same words to mean different things) is:
options: Honor the five frames of context — every Bible verse lives inside its paragraph, book, history, culture, and canon
mc.why: Correct. Cults speak fluent Bible. The defense is not to retreat from Scripture but to honor it more deeply — the five frames of context hold each verse in place, against every twister who quotes verses out of their setting.

mc.stem: The lesson's practical weekly schedule places "trace the canonical thread" on which day?
mc.why: Correct. Monday: immediate context. Tuesday: whole book. Wednesday: historical setting. Thursday: cultural details. Friday: canonical thread — what earlier Scripture stands behind, what later Scripture refers back. Saturday is for the sermon.

mc.stem: The closing image of this lesson is:
options: The pastor as a king who rules over his text
The pastor as a soldier who fights to the end
The pastor as a builder whose work will be tested by fire
The same Hand that saved the choir at West Side Baptist works through five small disciplines across one Bible week
mc.why: Correct. The choir was saved by fifteen small interruptions on a single night. Your congregation will be saved by five small disciplines across one Bible week. The same Hand is at work — quiet, providential, contextual.

fill.prompt: Read together, the fifteen small delays that kept the choir out of the exploding church show not accident but God's ____, His unseen care guiding every event.
The five layers of context are immediate, book, historical, cultural, and ____.
Lifted out of its paragraph, Jeremiah 29:11 becomes a refrigerator ____ that promises prosperity to anyone who claims it.
In the book of Esther the name of ____ is never mentioned, not once.
Haman was a descendant of the ____, the tribe that opposed Israel when they first approached the Promised Land.
In the Persian court, if the king did not extend his golden ____, anyone who came in uninvited was put to death.
The promise running underneath Esther is the covenant promise to ____ in Genesis 12.
The pastor who preaches only the lower story produces ____: be brave like Esther.
Mordecai asked Esther, "Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a ____ as this?"
Reading our own customs and values back into the lives of people who did not share them is the error of cultural ____.

sa.prompt: Tell the West Side Baptist Church gas-leak story (Beatrice, Nebraska, 1950) in your own words and explain what it illustrates about reading the Bible in context.
sa.model: On March 1, 1950, all fifteen members of the West Side Baptist choir in Beatrice were late for fifteen unrelated reasons, and the empty choir loft was spared when a gas leak blew up the church minutes later. Any single delay meant nothing; read together they reveal God's providence. So with Scripture: a verse pulled from its setting can mean anything, but read in context it says what its Author intended.

sa.prompt: Name the five layers of context the pastor must honor before preaching, and briefly explain what each layer is.
sa.model: The pastor must honor five frames of context before preaching: the immediate context of the surrounding verses, the book context of the whole book's purpose, the historical context of who was there and when, the cultural context of how they lived, and the canonical context of the whole Bible around the verse. Each layer guards the verse's meaning.

sa.prompt: Take Jeremiah 29:11 as your example. Explain how the prosperity-gospel misreading violates immediate context, and what the verse actually meant to its original readers.
sa.model: The prosperity reading rips Jeremiah 29:11 from its immediate context, where the very next verses speak of seventy years in Babylon. The promise was given to exiles facing long captivity, not to guarantee personal success today. Honoring the immediate context shows the verse means God's faithfulness through hardship, not a blank check for prosperity.

sa.prompt: Explain why the absence of God's name in the book of Esther is itself the key to reading the book — give the book-context interpretation.
sa.model: God's name is never mentioned in Esther, and that silence is itself the key to the book. The absence is deliberate: God is hidden but present, working His providence behind every scene — the insomnia, the banquet, the timing. Read at the book level, Esther teaches that the unnamed God rules even when He seems absent.

sa.prompt: Describe the historical context of the book of Esther — Persian Empire, Jews in exile, Haman as an Amalekite — and explain how this background changes the way we read the story.
sa.model: Esther is set around 480 B.C. in the Persian Empire under Xerxes, with the Jews scattered in exile across 127 provinces. Haman is an Amalekite, descended from Israel's ancient enemy since Sinai. Knowing this history, his plot to destroy the Jews is not random villainy but one more chapter in a thousand-year war — and the danger feels real.

sa.prompt: Give one example from the book of Esther where understanding the Persian cultural context changes the meaning of a scene the modern reader might otherwise miss.
sa.model: In Persian culture no one, not even the queen, could approach the king uninvited; without his golden scepter the visitor was put to death — so Esther's 'if I perish, I perish' was literal, not dramatic. And a king having the chronicles read aloud when he could not sleep was a normal custom, not a quirk; on that one night it became providence for Mordecai. Cultural context restores the weight of each scene.

sa.prompt: Identify the canonical-context promise that drives the book of Esther from underneath, and show how it is fulfilled in the story.
sa.model: The promise running underneath Esther is the covenant God made with Abraham in Genesis 12 — to bless those who bless his line and curse those who curse it. Haman, who plotted to curse and destroy the Jews, ends hanged on his own gallows, while the covenant people are preserved. Read canonically, Esther is the covenant keeping itself so the Messiah's line survives.

sa.prompt: Explain the distinction between the "lower story" and the "upper story" using Esther as your example, and describe what happens when a pastor preaches only one or the other.
sa.model: Every text has a lower story and an upper story. In Esther the lower story is what the palace sees — a sleepless king, a brave queen, an ambitious courtier. The upper story is what only God sees — His covenant keeping itself and the Messiah's line preserved. Preach only the lower story and you get moralism; preach only the upper and you get abstraction. The exegete must see both.

sa.prompt: Name the four serious errors that the discipline of context saves the pastor from, and briefly describe how each error fails to honor context.
sa.model: Context saves the pastor from four errors: proof-texting, snatching a verse to prove a point; moralism, turning every story into a lesson about being good; chronological flattening, ignoring where a passage sits in redemptive history; and cultural projection, reading our own customs back into the text. Each error fails to honor the context.

sa.prompt: Walk through the practical weekly schedule this lesson recommends (Monday through Saturday) and explain what discipline belongs on each day.
sa.model: The lesson spreads the five frames across one week: begin Monday with the immediate context, work through the book, historical, cultural, and canonical context from Tuesday through Friday, so that by Saturday the frames are hung and the sermon can be preached knowing the verse says what its Author intended. Five small disciplines across one Bible week.
